n: The Lord will remove every support Jerusalem leans on — food, water, and leadership. This likely points to sieges and exile, especially the later Babylonian conquest.

f.g: Every kind of support — props and crutches.

n: Soldiers, judges, prophets, wise people, and elders will all be taken away. When Babylon conquered Judah, it deported its leaders.

f.g: Here, a diviner — someone consulted for guidance.

n: Military officers, nobles, advisers, skilled craftsmen, and speakers will also disappear, leaving society without capable leaders.

f.g: A military officer over fifty men.

n: Immature and inexperienced people will rule over them. Without wise leaders, the nation will be governed by the foolish.
Society will break down: neighbors will oppress one another, and the young will disrespect the old, the lowly the honorable.
Things will be so bad that someone will beg a relative to be ruler just because he still owns a coat. 2 Nephi 13:6 reads “let not this ruin come under thy hand.”

f.w: let this ruin be under thy hand

n: But the relative will refuse, saying he has no food or clothing and can’t heal the nation’s wounds.
Jerusalem is ruined because its words and deeds defy the Lord, insulting His glorious presence.

f.w: provoke the eyes of his glory
f.g: Defy God openly, right before His face.

n: Their very faces show their guilt. Like Sodom, they flaunt their sins openly. 2 Nephi 13:9 says “they cannot hide it.”

f.g: Their facial expression; the look on their faces.

n: Assure the righteous that all will be well with them; they will enjoy the results of their good deeds.

f.w: eat the fruit of their doings

n: But woe to the wicked; they will receive what their actions deserve. 2 Nephi 13:11 adds plainly, “for they shall perish.”
Immature and weak leaders oppress the people. Those who should guide Israel are leading them astray and hiding the right path.

f.w: they which lead thee cause thee to err

n: The Lord stands up like a lawyer and a judge to bring His case against the people.
God puts the elders and princes on trial. They have devoured His vineyard — Israel — and filled their homes with goods stolen from the poor.
“What do you mean by crushing My people and grinding the faces of the poor?” God takes the abuse of the poor personally.

f.w: grind the faces of the poor
f.g: Crush them as with a millstone — oppress them mercilessly.

n: God now turns to Jerusalem’s proud upper-class women, who parade with heads held high and flirting eyes, mincing along with jingling ankle bracelets.

f.g: Ankle bracelets jingling as they walk.

n: Their pride will be humbled: disease and shame will replace their beauty. Captives were often stripped and shaved.
The Lord will strip away their jewelry. Verses 18–23 list about 21 fashion items of the day.
Necklaces, bracelets, and veils will be removed.
Headdresses, ankle chains, sashes, perfume bottles, and charms will be taken.
Signet rings and nose rings will be gone.
Fine festival clothing, cloaks, shawls, and purses will be lost.

f.g: Festive robes kept for special occasions.

n: Even mirrors, fine linen, turbans, and veils will be taken away. Isaiah isn’t condemning beauty but pride and luxury built while the poor suffered.
Everything will be reversed: stench instead of perfume, a rope instead of a sash, baldness instead of styled hair, sackcloth instead of fine robes, branding instead of beauty — the fate of captives.

f.g: A rope, used to lead captives.
Branding, as was done to slaves.

n: Their husbands and warriors will die in battle.

f.w: Thy men shall fall by the sword

n: Jerusalem’s gates — where people once gathered — will mourn, and the city, like a widow, will sit desolate on the ground.
